title: Working with Request and Response Objects
keywords: Working with Request and Response Objects
learning_outcomes: Describe Methods and headers and explain how it relates to Working with Request and Response Objects.
Demonstrate JSON responses in a small Node.js example and predict the observable result.
Test a failure, boundary, lifecycle, or version-compatibility case involving Text and binary responses.

content.intro: Working with Request and Response Objects is part of fetch web apis and external services. This lesson connects Methods and headers, JSON responses, Text and binary responses to a concrete Node.js example. Focus on the behavior you can observe, the assumptions the API makes, and one failure or boundary case.
content.why_it_matters: Fetch provides a standard request/response interface, but HTTP error statuses still need explicit application handling. Test non-2xx responses, malformed data, network failure, timeout, and cancellation using controlled responses.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Fetch provides a standard request/response interface, but HTTP error statuses still need explicit application handling. Check response.ok/status, parse the expected body type, and set timeouts or cancellation for remote calls.

content_blocks.title: Runtime and safety note
content_blocks.text: Teaching baseline: use a supported Node.js LTS release (Node.js 24 LTS as checked on 2026-10-13). The official releases page lists Node.js 26 as Current and Node.js 24/22 as LTS. Some advanced APIs, flags, permission behavior, embedded SQLite capabilities, module-loader hooks, and TypeScript integration are version-sensitive; verify the exact installed runtime. The Node.js 22 runtime available in the build-check environment is used only for syntax checks. This example is for learning and static validation, not for executing untrusted learner code inside CodeLeaf.

content.task: Create or inspect a small Node.js example for Working with Request and Response Objects. Include at least one listed subtopic, document the expected result, and verify a normal case plus a boundary or failure case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates a named lesson concept, rather than only mentioning the title.
Expected output or observable behavior is documented and reproducible.
At least one invalid, empty, timeout, resource, or failure case is handled or explained.
The solution does not put secrets in source code and does not execute untrusted code inside the production API process.
hints: Start with Methods and headers; identify the input, operation, and observable result.
Run the smallest relevant example in the selected Node.js release before adding frameworks or external services.
Test one failure or boundary case for JSON responses, then explain why the outcome is expected.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming fetch rejects automatically for every 4xx or 5xx response.
common_mistakes.why: The code may pass a simple demonstration yet fail with real inputs, resource limits, timing, or runtime differences.
common_mistakes.fix: Convert network and HTTP failures into explicit errors that callers can handle.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a snippet without checking its runtime, dependencies, input assumptions, or cleanup behavior.
common_mistakes.why: Node.js APIs and surrounding ecosystem tools have explicit version, trust, and resource boundaries.
common_mistakes.fix: State the environment and dependency assumptions, then rerun the example from a clean starting state.
